digest.top_line: ASTRO BCC/cSCC guideline: definitive BED10 70-93.5 conventional, adjuvant nodal RT 6000-6600 cGy, no concurrent carboplatin with adjuvant RT for resected cSCC.
digest.tldr: Four guidance documents, no new trial data. Skin carried the day with ASTRO's graded BCC/cSCC RT recommendations and GEC-ESTRO ACROP's depth-based brachy split (contact <5 mm, interstitial ≥5 mm). IMWG places RT for myeloma soft-tissue mass, not VCF stabilisation; COVID-era lung guidance lists 30Gy to 34Gy single-fraction SABR and 50Gy/5. Most rest on low-to-moderate or retrospective evidence.

sites.intro: Prior RT is not a contraindication to cement augmentation; RT treats soft-tissue mass, not VCF instability.

studies.name: IMWG consensus: cement augmentation for myeloma VCFs
studies.tldr: 4-8 wk window: IMWG advises offering BKP or PV for painful myeloma VCFs, with VAS ≥6 triaging to immediate augmentation and up to 3 levels per session.
details: 🔍 IMWG update of its 2008 cement-augmentation statement; panel consensus, not an outcome study

rows: Immediate augmentation; TLSO brace can bridge while systemic therapy starts
Chemo, bisphosphonate, analgesia first; augment if these fail or collapse risk rises

subdetails: Absolute: persistent pain from unhealed fracture confirmed on MRI STIR
Absolute: symptoms unresolved after 4 weeks of conservative care
Relative: T10-L2 fracture, progressive height loss, posterior wall or pedicle defect
Conditional/prophylactic: impending fracture, which the panel calls hard to determine
Soft-tissue mass or plasmacytoma unresolved with systemic therapy
Pts who cannot receive systemic therapy
Relapsed refractory disease
Poor performance status, palliative approach
Mass with severe pain
Plasmacytoma location precluding BKP or PV (posterior body near cord)

details: 🔍 RT shrinks soft-tissue myelomatous mass but does not stabilise the VCF
🔍 RT ineffective for bony neural compression; CT soft-tissue windows separate bone from tumour
🔍 Prior RT and prior RT dose are not contraindications to cement augmentation
🔍 Up to 3 levels per session; more only with caution given pulmonary cement embolus
🔍 Avoid instrumentation where possible: metalwork failure in weak bone, infection during immunosuppression
🔗 CAFE RCT: 134 cancer pts, 49 MM; 22 randomised to BKP, 27 to NSM
⚠️ Myeloma-specific randomised evidence rests on CAFE's 49-pt MM subset
⚠️ Osteoporotic sham-controlled trials (Kallmes, Buchbinder) showed no pain benefit; panel attributes this to selection and facet pain
studies.significance: The RT boundary is explicit: RT shrinks a soft-tissue myelomatous mass but neither stabilises a VCF nor relieves bony neural compression, and prior RT or its dose does not contraindicate later cement. That narrows RT for painful myeloma VCFs to unresolved plasmacytoma, no systemic option, or posterior-element disease precluding BKP/PV, with marrow sparing as a stated aim.
studies.monday_clinic: In a myeloma pt with a painful, MRI-confirmed unhealed VCF and no soft-tissue canal mass, this supports cement augmentation over RT for fracture pain; it does not apply to soft-tissue cord compression, where steroids, systemic therapy and RT come first.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: International Myeloma Working Group consensus statement updating the **2008** recommendations on vertebral cement augmentation in light of newer published data. No new patient data.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: RT to be used **judiciously and sparingly** to spare marrow. Effective for a **soft-tissue mass**, not for bony compression, and **does not stabilise the VCF**. Prior RT and its dose are **not contraindications** to later PV or BKP.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: **CAFE** is the one randomised trial cited for cancer VCFs, with only 49 MM pts. The osteoporotic sham-controlled trials (Kallmes, Buchbinder) were null for pain, which the panel attributes to excluding the sickest pts and enrolling facet-pain cases.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Systemic therapy is framed as the most important modality, with bracing to bridge the first 1-2 cycles and augmentation if fracture pain persists. Metalwork is to be avoided where possible given failure and infection risk.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents myeloma pts with painful VCFs, with or without neurological deficit. Does not represent osteoporotic VCFs or solid-tumour spinal metastases, where the panel notes the myeloma spine may behave differently.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: VAS tiers are pragmatic triage, not validated cut points. BKP vs PV, timing relative to induction, and impending-fracture prediction are all deferred to future randomised trials.

studies.interpretation:
This is a panel position, and its weight depends on how much myeloma-specific evidence sits beneath it. The randomised core is CAFE, which compared BKP with non-surgical management in a mixed cancer population; only 49 of its 134 pts had myeloma, split 22 to BKP and 27 to NSM. Everything else the panel cites for myeloma is prospective single-arm or retrospective series, plus osteoporosis data. The recommendation that painful myeloma VCFs be offered BKP or PV within 4-8 weeks is therefore an extrapolation from a small randomised subset and a body of uncontrolled experience, delivered with the confidence a consensus format confers.

The panel has to contend with the two sham-controlled osteoporosis trials, Kallmes and Buchbinder, that found no pain benefit for vertebroplasty. Its rebuttal is selection: the pts most in need may have declined randomisation, and those enrolled may have had facet-mediated rather than fracture pain. That argument is plausible but untested, and it cuts both ways in myeloma. If facet pain after kyphotic deformity is common, some pts referred for cement would do as well with a facet injection, which the panel itself concedes. The insistence on MRI with STIR and T1 sequences to confirm an unhealed fracture, often with a cleft, is the practical safeguard against treating the wrong pain generator.

For a radiation oncologist the statement is a boundary-setting document. It casts RT as the right tool for a soft-tissue myelomatous mass, including cord compression without bony encroachment, and the wrong tool for mechanical fracture pain, because RT does not stabilise the vertebral body. It asks for sparing use to protect marrow and expects steroid plus novel-agent combinations to reduce palliative RT demand. That is an expectation about practice, not a measured result. The only RT comparison cited, additional kyphoplasty versus additional radiation or systemic therapy, comes from a single referenced study with no effect size in the text, so the RT-versus-cement question for myeloma VCF pain has not been tested head to head.

The most portable line is that prior RT and its dose do not contraindicate cement. It removes a common hesitation when an irradiated level stays painful, as in the illustrated case of T10 BKP after dexamethasone, RT and 2 cycles of chemotherapy. What the statement does not settle is whether BKP beats PV in myeloma, the right timing relative to induction, and how to identify an impending fracture; the panel defers all three to future randomised trials. The VAS tiers are triage conventions rather than validated thresholds, and the panel's own indications table says pain is not defined by a specific VAS number. Read it as a reasonable default pathway that clarifies where RT stops being the answer, not as evidence that cement outperforms RT for any defined myeloma population.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: RT is positioned for soft-tissue mass, unresolved plasmacytoma or posterior-element disease precluding cement, not for mechanical VCF pain, since it does not stabilise the vertebra. Prior RT or its dose does not contraindicate later augmentation, so an irradiated level that stays painful remains a cement candidate.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Systemic anti-myeloma therapy is named the most important modality, with augmentation timed after 1-2 cycles when performance status, sepsis or hyperviscosity contraindicate it up front. Procedures need coordinating with the treating haematologist to avoid therapy-related anaemia, leukopaenia and thrombocytopaenia.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: The panel argues against spinal metalwork in myeloma: secondary osteoporosis raises failure risk and immunosuppression raises infection risk. Cement supports the anterior and middle columns; urgent decompression is reserved for cord or cauda equina compression with deficit, or bony encroachment that steroids, chemotherapy and RT cannot reverse.

open_questions: BKP vs PV vs NSM head to head in myeloma VCFs
Optimal timing of augmentation relative to induction therapy
How to predict impending fracture in the myeloma spine

sites.intro: Two RT guidance documents, both built on retrospective or single-institution series with no randomised surgery vs RT data.

studies.name: GEC-ESTRO ACROP skin brachytherapy recommendations
studies.tldr: Depth sets the technique: contact BT for skin tumours <5 mm deep, interstitial for ≥5 mm or curved surfaces; no standard dose schedule endorsed.
details: 🔍 GEC-ESTRO ACROP recommendation document, Radiother Oncol 2018; covers technique, CTV margins, dose and QA for skin BT

details.text: 🔍 Technique selection by lesion depth and surface

rows: Regular surfaces; flaps for larger volumes; custom moulds for nose, pinna, hand, fingers
GTV→CTV at least 5 mm, plus 1–2 mm PTV
Thickness 5 mm or more, irregular surfaces
Catheters 8–12 mm apart, at least 3 mm under skin
BCC, poorly defined, large, infiltrative, morphoeic or sclerotic
20–30 mm peripheral; deep 5–10 mm below visible extension
Whole surgical site; margins per histopathology

details.text: 💊 Listed surface BT schedules by applicator (menu of published practice, not ranked)

subdetails: LDR: 60 Gy at the 85% reference isodose over 4–6 days
HDR/PDR: twice daily, 2.5–4 Gy per fx, at least 6 h apart
PDR alternative: 0.8–1 Gy per pulse

details: 📐 Valencia: typical prescription depth 3 mm with skin surface dose around 135%
⚠️ Plastic cap omitted → skin dose 2.5× (Valencia) and 10× (Leipzig) higher

details.text: 📊 Keloids: post-excision HDR, single catheter placed at surgery
subdetails: Catheter at least 4 mm under the skin
Prescription 4–5 mm from the source
5–6 Gy × 3 fx or 5 Gy × 4 fx
First session same day as surgery, always before 24 h

details.text: 🔗 Keloid systematic review cited: modality vs mean dose and recurrence

details: ⚠️ Evidence base mostly single-institution small series; authors note RCTs and meta-analyses are lacking
⚠️ Authors state no standard schedule can be recommended; doses rest on experience, not evidence
studies.significance: The dosimetric fine print gates safety: with the Valencia applicator prescribed at 3 mm, skin surface dose runs around 135%, and omitting the plastic cap raises skin dose 2.5× (Valencia) or 10× (Leipzig). Recording surface dose, not only prescription-depth dose, is what lets late toxicity be compared across schedules.
studies.monday_clinic: In a NMSC under 5 mm deep on a flat or small surface, this supports contact BT (mould, flap or shielded applicator) as the technique; it does not extend to lesions 5 mm or thicker or on curved facial surfaces, where interstitial implant is the stated option.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: GEC-ESTRO ACROP recommendation document (Radiother Oncol 2018) drawing on published series and an ABS report; **no new outcome data** and no formal grading of evidence stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Contact techniques prescribe to **3–5 mm** (moulds/flaps) or **3–4 mm** (shielded applicators); interstitial catheters sit **8–12 mm apart** and at least **3 mm** under the skin. Shielded applicators need at least **5 mm** GTV→CTV plus **1–2 mm** PTV, and a CT with surface markers is the standard for moulds and implants.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents BCC, SCC, Merkel cell and post-excision keloids treated with surface or interstitial BT, including elderly and frail pts. Does not represent eyelid lesions where function can be preserved surgically, for which surgery is the stated gold standard.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The anchor cited is the **ABS report** summarizing **19 published protocols**, with local control in the **90–100%** range. Head-to-head data vs surgery are limited to a nasal vestibule HDR comparison (**no difference in locoregional control or survival**, better function and cosmesis) and an electronic BT vs Mohs **matched-pair cohort**.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Schedule grid mixes LDR, HDR and electronic sources with different gradients (**8%** vs **12% per mm**), so totals are not interchangeable. BED is set aside for surface work because overall treatment time varies, leaving no common dose currency.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The firm content is geometric and dosimetric; the dose content is a **menu, not a ranking**. Hypofractionation in frail pts is accepted **at the cost of reduced cosmesis**, which is the trade a reader is actually making when choosing once-weekly schedules.

studies.interpretation:
This document reads best as a technique manual issued under a guideline banner. Its firm content is geometric and dosimetric: which applicator family fits which lesion depth and surface, how far catheters sit from the skin, how wide the CTV extends by histology, and what happens to skin dose when setup details slip. Its dose-fractionation content is deliberately soft. The authors say outright that no standard schedule can be recommended and that prescriptions rest more on experience than on evidence, then list the regimens in common use. A reader should treat that schedule grid as a catalogue of published practice, not as a ranked recommendation, and should not infer equivalence between rows simply because they share a table.

There is little to set this against in the trial sense. The authors concede that randomized trials, systematic reviews and meta-analyses are missing and that most series come from single institutions with small numbers. The nearest anchor is the ABS report summarizing 19 protocols, with local control between 90 and 100%. Those figures come from selected cohorts, often elderly, treated by experienced centres, and a less selected population with thicker or poorly defined lesions would plausibly sit lower. The comparisons with surgery are thin: a nasal vestibule HDR series showing no difference in locoregional control or survival but better function and cosmesis, and an electronic BT versus Mohs matched-pair cohort. Matching is not randomization; lesion size, site and histologic subtype can steer pts toward either arm. On eyelid tumours the document itself names surgery as the gold standard and positions BT for cases where functional structures cannot be preserved.

The most consequential methodological point sits in the dose-calculation section, not the conclusions. Every surface technique delivers more at the skin than at the prescription point, and the excess depends on bolus thickness, prescription depth and gradient. With the Valencia applicator prescribed at 3 mm, surface dose runs around 135%; gradients differ between devices (8% per mm for Esteya, 12% per mm for the others); and a missing plastic cap multiplies skin dose 2.5-fold or 10-fold. Two centres using the same nominal schedule can therefore deliver materially different skin doses, which confounds any cross-series comparison of cosmesis or late toxicity. That is why the request to record surface dose matters more than any single regimen: without it, published control and cosmesis rates cannot be mapped onto a dose-response.

What the document changes is selection and setup: contact BT without anaesthesia for tumours under 5 mm deep, interstitial implants at 5 mm or more or on curved facial surfaces, histology-based margins borrowed for SCC from NCCN, and same-day post-excision HDR for keloids. What it leaves untouched is whether BT should displace excision for a resectable lesion, which dose per fraction best balances control against long-term cosmesis, and how much cosmetic cost is acceptable when hypofractionating for frail pts. The guidance would be wrong in practice if large-fraction schedules such as 10 Gy weekly or 7 Gy twice weekly produced late skin changes that protracted schedules avoid; late skin effects take years to emerge, and nothing in the document establishes long-term cosmesis by schedule.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Lesion depth drives the technique: contact BT below 5 mm without anaesthesia, interstitial at 5 mm or more or on curved facial surfaces, with catheters at least 3 mm under the skin. Surface dose exceeds the prescription in every contact technique, so documenting it is the practical change for an RT program building a skin BT service.

open_questions: Optimal dose per fraction for skin surface brachytherapy
Randomized comparison of skin brachytherapy vs surgery
Long-term cosmesis of large-fraction schedules in frail pts

studies.name: ASTRO guideline: definitive and postoperative RT for BCC and cSCC
studies.tldr: The guideline gives explicit strength and evidence grades for definitive RT, PORT, nodal RT, BED10 dose ranges and concurrent systemic therapy in non-metastatic BCC and cSCC. Most rest on low-to-moderate evidence.
details: 🧭 Society guideline, not a trial: 5 key questions, graded strength × quality of evidence (QoE)

rows: Surgery would compromise function or cosmesis

details.text: 🔍 KQ2 · PORT indications, cSCC vs BCC

rows: Gross perineural spread, clinical or radiologic
Locally advanced/neglected, into bone or muscle
Clinically apparent nodes → lymphadenectomy + adjuvant RT (except single <3 cm cervical node, no ECE)
Definitive nodal RT only if inoperable or unresectable
Imaging + SLNB to guide nodal RT, high-risk cSCC
Elective nodal RT, cSCC thickness >6 mm, only if primary field overlaps basin
Adjuvant after lymphadenectomy: 6000-6600 cGy at 180-200 cGy/fx
Elective, no lymphadenectomy: 5000-5400 cGy at 180-200 cGy/fx

details.text: 📐 KQ4 · primary-site BED10 ranges (Strong rec, Low QoE)

details: 🔍 Modality (ELS, HDR brachy, electrons, MV photons) left to tumor depth, contour and location
📐 Task force: no data support 6600 over 6000 cGy for positive margins or ECE

subdetails: Resected locally advanced cSCC: concurrent carboplatin with adjuvant RT not recommended (Strong, Moderate)
Unresected locally advanced cSCC: concurrent drug with definitive RT conditionally recommended (Low)
Hedgehog inhibitors, cemiplimab framed as palliative; avoid where curative surgery or RT feasible

details: ⚠️ AJCC eighth edition skin staging is head and neck only; trunk/limb recs are extrapolated
⚠️ No randomized surgery vs RT data; definitive-RT recs rest on retrospective and single-arm series
studies.significance: The nodal dose ceiling is the practical read. The adjuvant dose is 6000-6600 cGy after lymphadenectomy, and the panel says no data support 6600 cGy even for positive margins or ECE. It also exempts a single <3 cm cervical node without ECE from adjuvant RT, so de-escalation in both directions has explicit cover.
studies.monday_clinic: In resected cSCC with close or positive margins that cannot be re-excised, this supports PORT as a Strong recommendation. The same margin scenario in BCC gets only a conditional recommendation, which leaves room for shared decision-making.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: ASTRO task force guideline: systematic MEDLINE review (May 1988 through June 2018) graded by **strength × QoE**. Consensus came from a modified Delphi process with a **≥75% agreement threshold** (≥90% for expert opinion). Endorsed by AAPM, ABS, ACR, AHNS and SSO.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Adults with **non-metastatic invasive BCC or cSCC** treated with curative-intent RT. Re-irradiation, palliation and dosimetric studies were excluded. Minimum cohort size was ≥100 pts for KQ1, ≥50 for KQ2 to 4 and ≥15 for KQ5.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Primary-site dosing is given as **BED10 ranges**, not fixed schedules. Definitive: conventional 70-93.5, hypofractionated 56-88. Postoperative: conventional 59.5-79.2, hypofractionated 56-70.2. Gross perineural spread on imaging gets definitive-equivalent dose, preferably conventionally fractionated.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Cisplatin with adjuvant RT has randomized support in **mucosal head and neck SCC**. The one randomized trial in high-risk resected cSCC found **no benefit** from weekly carboplatin added to PORT, which is why the guideline recommends against it. Nodal dosing and the 6-week start window are extrapolated from mucosal H&N practice.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents adults with non-metastatic invasive BCC or cSCC of the head and neck, trunk or limbs receiving definitive or postoperative curative-intent RT. Does not represent metastatic disease, re-irradiation, palliation, or mucosal H&N, vulvar, penile or perianal skin carcinoma.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: AJCC eighth edition skin staging covers **head and neck only**, so the T3/T4 PORT trigger has no staged equivalent on the trunk or limbs. Microscopic perineural invasion has **no recommendation**; only gross spread is addressed.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Strength and evidence diverge on purpose: several **Strong** recommendations sit on **Low** QoE and reflect panel conviction, not measured benefit. The cSCC vs BCC split in PORT strength is the guideline's most usable distinction. The panel considered recommending against routine elective nodal RT but judged the data insufficient either way.

studies.interpretation:
This document is best read as a codification of radiation practice that already existed, not as a shift in it. The evidence review itself concedes that few well-conducted modern randomized trials support RT in BCC or cSCC, so most recommendations rest on retrospective series and expert opinion. The grading is honest about that. Several recommendations pair a Strong label with Low quality of evidence, including PORT for cSCC with uncorrectable close or positive margins and the KQ4 BED10 ranges. ASTRO's grading system separates strength from evidence quality on purpose, but a reader should take a Strong/Low recommendation as panel conviction rather than a measured effect.

The most useful asymmetry for a radiation oncologist is between histologies after surgery. The same scenarios (margins that cannot be corrected surgically, recurrence after a margin-negative resection) earn a Strong recommendation in cSCC and only a Conditional one in BCC. The stated rationale is that cSCC carries far greater regional and nodal risk. For a post-excision referral, that split is explicit cover for shared decision-making in BCC while treating the equivalent cSCC.

The nodal section leans heavily on mucosal head and neck practice. The adjuvant dose of 6000-6600 cGy, the statement that no data support escalating to 6600 cGy for positive margins or extranodal extension, and the start window of within 6 weeks of surgery are all extrapolations. The elective nodal recommendation is deliberately narrow: cSCC thicker than 6 mm, and only when the primary field already overlaps the draining basin. The text records that the panel considered recommending against routine elective nodal RT but judged the data insufficient. The median 5-year regional relapse-free survival of 99% it cites comes from selected retrospective series and cannot separate treatment effect from patient selection.

On systemic therapy, the one randomized input is negative: weekly carboplatin added to PORT did not help high-risk resected cSCC. That is why the guideline declines to carry the mucosal SCC chemoradiation paradigm across. The advice to avoid hedgehog inhibitors and cemiplimab where curative surgery or RT is feasible reflects their palliative approval status at publication. It is also the section most likely to be outdated by later perioperative immunotherapy data, and the guideline commits to replacement or reaffirmation within 5 years of publication, so a reader should check for an update before relying on KQ5.

Two structural limits affect how well the recommendations transfer. AJCC eighth edition staging for skin covers only the head and neck, so the T3/T4 PORT trigger has no staged equivalent on the trunk or limbs, where the panel also notes that salvage re-resection is less morbid. And giving BED10 ranges rather than fixed schedules keeps flexibility across ELS, HDR brachytherapy, electrons and MV photons but leaves fractionation unstandardized. The task force names standardization as a research priority, along with microscopic perineural invasion, which it leaves without a recommendation.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Nodal dosing has an explicit ceiling: 6000-6600 cGy after lymphadenectomy, with no data supporting 6600 cGy for positive margins or ECE. Elective nodal RT is narrowed to cSCC thicker than 6 mm with a primary field overlapping the basin. Primary-site dosing is given as BED10 ranges, so modality choice stays open.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Concurrent carboplatin with adjuvant RT for resected locally advanced cSCC is a Strong recommendation against, based on a negative randomized trial. Concurrent drug therapy with definitive RT is only conditionally recommended for unresected disease, on Low QoE. Hedgehog inhibitors and cemiplimab were positioned as palliative where curative local therapy is feasible.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Clinically apparent nodes go to therapeutic lymphadenectomy first, with definitive nodal RT reserved for inoperable or unresectable disease. Imaging plus SLNB is conditionally recommended for high-risk cSCC to guide nodal RT. PORT triggers in cSCC hinge on whether close or positive margins can be corrected surgically.

sites.intro: Shortened curative schedules rest on radiobiological equivalence and retrospective series, not randomised comparison.

studies.name: Reduced fractionation in lung RT during COVID-19
studies.tldr: COVID-era consensus on shorter curative lung RT: 30Gy to 34Gy single-fraction SABR, 50Gy in 5 fractions, and 15-fraction schedules modelled against 55Gy/20.
details: 🔍 Clinical Oncology 2020 guidance for curative-intent lung RT under pandemic resource limits
🔍 Built from literature review, published series and centre audits, not new trial data
📊 Reduced-fractionation options cited, by setting

details.text: ⚠️ Chest wall toxicity in a cited single-fraction series
subdetails: 30.6% for lesions abutting the chest wall
8.2% for tumours ≤1cm from the chest wall
Overall grade ≥3 chest wall toxicity 1.4%

details: 📊 SABR for larger tumours: OAR constraints must be met as for lesions ≤5cm
⚠️ One cited larger-tumour SABR series: 30% grade ≥3 toxicity, pneumonitis most common
📊 One cited concurrent chemoRT cohort: 25% ≥grade 3 oesophagitis, 10% ≥grade 3 pneumonitis
🔗 Cited retrospective hypofractionation data reported outcomes comparable to ≥60Gy conventional fractionation
⚠️ Most schedules rest on radiobiological equivalence and retrospective series, not randomised comparison
studies.significance: The transferable part is the radiobiology: at α/β of 10, 52Gy/15 is quoted as isoeffective with 55Gy/20 for tumour control, and at α/β of 3, 50Gy/15 is isotoxic for late effects. That is a modelled bridge from 20 to 15 fractions, not outcome data, and OAR constraints still gate it.
studies.monday_clinic: In a small peripheral lung tumour clear of the chest wall, this supports single-fraction SABR as a reduced-visit option; it does not extend to lesions abutting the chest wall, where cited chest wall toxicity was 30.6%.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Consensus guidance from lung clinical oncologists, built from a literature search plus published and unpublished centre audits. **No new patient data.**

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Options span **30Gy to 34Gy single-fraction** SABR for small peripheral tumours, **50Gy in 5 fractions** (Glasgow, RTOG 0813 constraints), 15-fraction radical schedules modelled against **55Gy/20**, and **40Gy in 15 fractions** with concurrent or sequential chemotherapy.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Cited single-fraction data put chest wall toxicity at **30.6%** for lesions abutting the chest wall vs **8.2%** for tumours ≤1cm from it. One concurrent chemoRT cohort reported **25%** ≥grade 3 oesophagitis and **10%** ≥grade 3 pneumonitis.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The 5-fraction SABR recommendation leans on **RTOG 0813** dose constraints rather than new dose-finding. Hypofractionated radical schedules are justified by isoeffect calculation and retrospective series reporting outcomes comparable to ≥60Gy conventional RT.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents lung cancer pts planned for curative-intent RT when departments need fewer visits. Does not represent a tested replacement for standard fractionation outside resource-constrained settings.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Toxicity numbers come from mixed cited cohorts with different regimens and selection, so they are not directly comparable across rows. The isotoxicity claims depend on assumed α/β values.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The document reframes fractionation as a risk-benefit trade under infection risk, not a new standard. It does not settle whether 15-fraction concurrent chemoRT matches standard schedules for late toxicity.

studies.interpretation:
This is a guidance document, and it should be read as one. Its job was to give lung radiotherapy departments a defensible set of shorter schedules at a moment when every hospital visit carried infection risk and staffing was unpredictable. What it offers a radiation oncologist now is less a set of rules than a map of how far fractionation can be compressed before the evidence thins out.

The strongest ground is stereotactic treatment of small peripheral tumours. Single-fraction delivery of 30Gy to 34Gy has the most direct support, and the guidance pairs it with a sharp chest wall caveat: in a cited series, chest wall toxicity ran 30.6% for lesions abutting the chest wall against 8.2% for tumours close to it, with overall grade ≥3 chest wall toxicity of 1.4%. That gradient is the practical message. Single-fraction SABR is a reasonable compression for the right geometry and a poor one when the target sits on the chest wall. The 50Gy in 5 fraction schedule used in Glasgow is anchored to RTOG 0813 constraints, which gives it a recognisable safety frame.

The radical conventional-to-hypofractionated step is weaker ground. The case for moving from 55Gy/20 to 15 fractions is radiobiological: 52Gy/15 is quoted as isoeffective for tumour control at an α/β of 10, and 50Gy/15 as isotoxic for late effects at an α/β of 3. That is internally consistent but entirely dependent on the assumed α/β values and on the linear-quadratic model holding across the dose range. A reader should treat these as planning hypotheses, not demonstrated equivalence.

Chemoradiation is where caution matters most. The cited cohort reporting 25% ≥grade 3 oesophagitis and 10% ≥grade 3 pneumonitis with concurrent chemotherapy is a reminder that compressing fractionation with a systemic backbone concentrates acute toxicity. The 40Gy in 15 fraction option is described as used concurrently and sequentially, but the supporting data are retrospective and heterogeneous.

Methodologically, the document is honest about its base: most hypofractionation data are retrospective single-institution series. The toxicity figures across sections come from different cohorts, regimens and selection, so they cannot be lined up against each other. For larger tumours the guidance holds the line on organ-at-risk constraints, noting one series with 30% grade ≥3 toxicity, pneumonitis most common.

What it changes is the menu, not the default. Outside a resource crisis, it supports single-fraction SABR for well-placed small tumours and gives a modelled rationale for 15-fraction radical schedules; it does not establish that those schedules match standard fractionation for late toxicity in chemoradiation.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The usable content is the fractionation map: 30Gy to 34Gy single-fraction SABR when the tumour is clear of the chest wall, and 52Gy/15 or 50Gy/15 modelled against 55Gy/20. Chest wall proximity (30.6% vs 8.2% toxicity) is the geometry gate for single fraction.

The role of cement augmentation with percutaneous vertebroplasty and balloon kyphoplasty for the treatment of vertebral compression fractures in multiple myeloma: a consensus statement from the International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG)
papers.abstract: Abstract Multiple myeloma (MM) represents approximately 15% of haematological malignancies and most of the patients present with bone involvement. Focal or diffuse spinal osteolysis may result in significant morbidity by causing painful progressive vertebral compression fractures (VCFs) and deformities. Advances in the systemic treatment of myeloma have achieved high response rates and prolonged the survival significantly. Early diagnosis and management of skeletal events contribute to improving the prognosis and quality of life of MM patients. The management of patients with significant pain due to VCFs in the acute phase is not standardised. While some patients are successfully treated conservatively, and pain relief is achieved within a few weeks, a large percentage has disabling pain and morbidity and hence they are considered for surgical intervention. Balloon kyphoplasty and percutaneous vertebroplasty are minimally invasive procedures which have been shown to relieve pain and restore function. Despite increasing positive evidence for the use of these procedures, the indications, timing, efficacy, safety and their role in the treatment algorithm of myeloma spinal disease are yet to be elucidated. This paper reports an update of the consensus statement from the International Myeloma Working Group on the role of cement augmentation in myeloma patients with VCFs.
